finding.claim: Authorization identity is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header without signature, session, or proxy verification, so any reachable client can act as any user holding a grant on a file and delete or rename it.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, read in load_user (before_request) at views.py:11
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") at views.py:17 gating del STORE[fid] at views.py:18; is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:25 gating rename at views.py:27

trace.note: ensure_allowed called with the forged g.user for DELETE /files/<fid>
is_allowed looks up resource["grants"][user] using the forged name
ensure_allowed aborts 403 only when the forged name lacks the action
file deleted when the check passes
rename path uses the same forged identity against write grant

finding.guards_checked: None on the path. Header is not signed or matched to a server-side session; no proxy-stripping logic in the corpus. acl.is_allowed denies a missing user (grants.get(None, []) is empty), so unauthenticated requests without the header are blocked, but a forged header bypasses this. Reachability is unverified: no bind address or proxy config is in scope. Finding downgrades to MEDIUM or closes if a trusted proxy guarantees the header is stripped and set upstream.
finding.repro: curl -X DELETE http://<host>/files/<fid> -H 'X-Session-User-Verified: <granted-user>'  (non-granted or missing user gets 403; granted name gets 200 {"ok": true})

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:11 assigns g.user straight from the request header with no signature, session, or proxy check. views.py:17 and views.py:25 call the ACL checks with that value. acl.py:5 is a pure grant lookup, and acl.py:8-10 aborts 403 only when the claimed name lacks the action. The only protection is that a missing header yields user None, which has no grants (acl.py:5). A forged header with a granted username bypasses it.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: views.py:11 trusts the header, views.py:17-18 delete on ensure_allowed(g.user) (acl.py:8-10) with no other check, and views.py:25-27 rename via is_allowed, so any client that sends a granted username can act as that user. The attacker is anonymous, and the only open question is deployment: if a trusted proxy strips and re-sets this header upstream, the finding drops to MEDIUM, but nothing in the corpus shows that.

finding.claim: Unknown file IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500), while existing but inaccessible IDs return 403, letting a client probe whether a given file ID exists.
finding.source: URL path parameter fid in DELETE /files/<fid> and POST /files/<fid>/rename
finding.sink: STORE[fid] dictionary lookup at views.py:16 and views.py:24 with no existence check

trace.note: f = STORE[fid] raises KeyError for an unknown fid
403 returned only when the fid exists and the ACL check fails

finding.guards_checked: No existence check or error handler before the lookup. Impact is limited to existence probing and matters only if IDs are guessable. Retained at LOW under triage Check 8 (non-actionable information disclosure).

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:16 and views.py:24 are bare `STORE[fid]` lookups with no existence check, and no error handler exists in views.py or acl.py. The only 403 path is acl.py:10 (`abort(403)` via ensure_allowed), reached only after the lookup succeeds, so an unknown fid yields a KeyError (HTTP 500) before any ACL check.
verdict.reason:
views.py:16 raises KeyError for unknown fid, while acl.py:9-10 (reached via views.py:17) aborts 403 only for existing files, so the 500-vs-403 difference is a real existence oracle reachable by any client that can send requests (g.user may be None per views.py:11). The impact is limited to ID-existence probing, consistent with the candidate's LOW rating.</reason>
